questions.q: What ServiceAccount does a Pod get if its spec doesn't specify one?
options: No ServiceAccount at all — it runs with no identity
The default ServiceAccount of its namespace, assigned automatically
The ServiceAccount of whichever user ran kubectl apply
A new random ServiceAccount is created for it
questions.explain: Any Pod that doesn't set serviceAccountName is automatically assigned the default ServiceAccount of its namespace, which typically has no RBAC permissions bound to it.

questions.q: In a RoleBinding, how do you bind a Role to a ServiceAccount rather than a human user?
options: It's not possible — Roles can only bind to Users
Set the subjects entry's kind to ServiceAccount, with its name and namespace
Add the ServiceAccount's token directly into the Role's rules
ServiceAccounts automatically inherit every Role in their namespace
questions.explain: A RoleBinding's subjects list can name a User, Group, or ServiceAccount — for a ServiceAccount, kind is set to ServiceAccount with its name and namespace.

questions.q: How does a Pod actually use a ServiceAccount's permissions at runtime?
options: The permissions are copied into the Pod's environment variables as plain text
Kubernetes mounts the ServiceAccount's token into the container; the app presents that token to the API server, which checks it against the bound RBAC rules
The Pod's image must be rebuilt with the permissions baked in
Permissions apply only to kubectl commands run from outside the Pod
questions.explain: The ServiceAccount's token is mounted into the container's filesystem; the application uses it to authenticate API calls, which the API server authorizes against that ServiceAccount's RBAC bindings.

questions.q: Why would Northbridge set automountServiceAccountToken: false on its checkout Pods?
options: To make checkout Pods start faster
Checkout Pods serve HTTP traffic and never call the Kubernetes API, so mounting an unused token only adds something an attacker could steal if the Pod were compromised
It is required for every Pod in a Deployment
To grant checkout Pods more RBAC permissions
questions.explain: Disabling automatic token mounting for Pods that never call the API shrinks the blast radius if that Pod is ever compromised — there is simply no token to steal.

questions.q: Why create a dedicated ServiceAccount for catalog-sync instead of leaving it on the namespace's default ServiceAccount?
options: Dedicated ServiceAccounts run containers with more CPU
It lets catalog-sync's specific API permissions (e.g. read ConfigMaps) be scoped and audited separately from everything else sharing default
The default ServiceAccount cannot be used by any Pod
It changes which namespace the Pod runs in
questions.explain: A dedicated ServiceAccount keeps a Pod's specific permissions isolated and auditable, rather than mixing them in with every other Pod relying on the shared default identity.
